New Hampshire property tax is assessed and collected at the local level, and owners can appeal an assessment.

What the official sources say

  • Step one: apply in writing to the selectmen or assessors for an abatement by March 1 following the date of notice of tax. (RSA 76:16, I(b); source)
  • Selectmen or assessors must grant or deny the abatement application in writing by July 1 after the notice of tax date; failure to respond is a denial. (RSA 76:16, II; source)
  • If the notice of tax is on or before Dec. 31, the BTLA appeal deadline is September 1 (but no earlier than the municipal decision or July 1); if after Dec. 31, it is 8 months after the notice of tax. (Property Tax | Board of Tax and Land Appeals; source)
  • BTLA appeal filing fee is $65 by check or money order payable to Treasurer, State of NH. (Property Tax | Board of Tax and Land Appeals; source)
  • After 2 years from execution of an unredeemed real estate tax lien, the collector executes a tax deed to the lienholder. (RSA 80:76, I; source)
  • A municipality may refuse a tax deed; the lien then remains indefinitely and the right of redemption continues with interest. (RSA 80:76, II-a, III; source)

Last updated November 14, 2026.

New Hampshire evictions follow notice and court steps set by state law.

What the official sources say

  • For residential tenancies, 30 days' eviction notice suffices; 7 days if the reason is nonpayment, substantial damage, behavior affecting health/safety, or domestic violence cotenant termination. (RSA 540:3, II; source)
  • Notice must state the reason with specificity; nonpayment notices must advise of the right to cure under RSA 540:9. (RSA 540:3, III-IV; source)
  • Restricted property may be terminated only for listed reasons including nonpayment, substantial damage, material lease violation, other good cause, and lease expiration with 60 days' notice for leases of 12 months or longer. (RSA 540:2, II; source)
  • After the notice expires the landlord obtains a landlord-tenant writ; the return day is 7 days from service; if the tenant appears a hearing is set within 10 days. (Navigating the NH Eviction Process | NH Judicial Branch; source)
  • Tenant may cure nonpayment by paying back rent plus $15, up to three times in 12 months; money judgments in these cases are limited to $1500. (Navigating the NH Eviction Process | NH Judicial Branch; source)
  • Court may stay the writ of possession up to 90 days if the tenant pays rent weekly; notice of intent to appeal is due within 7 days of the notice of judgment. (Navigating the NH Eviction Process | NH Judicial Branch; source)
  • A refusal of a rent increase noticed 30 days ahead, and legitimate business or economic reasons, can constitute 'other good cause' for terminating a restricted tenancy. (RSA 540:2, IV-V; source)
  • For residential tenancies, 30 days' eviction notice is generally required. (RSA 540:3, II; source)
  • Lease expiration is a ground only for leases of 12 months or longer, with 60 days' written notice and possessory action filed within 6 months. (RSA 540:2, II(i); source)

Last updated November 14, 2026.

New Hampshire probate runs through the courts named in the sources below.

What the official sources say

  • Waiver of Administration under RSA 553:32 is a simplified probate process for testate or intestate estates; no inventory, fiduciary bond or accounting is required. (What is Waiver of Administration? | NH Judicial Branch; source)
  • The Waiver of Full Administration Statement (NHJB-2144-Pe) is filed no sooner than 6 months nor more than one year after the administrator's appointment, with no outstanding debts or claims. (What is Waiver of Administration? | NH Judicial Branch; source)
  • Transfers by devise, intestate succession, or death of a joint tenant are exempt from the real estate transfer tax. (RSA 78-B:2, XI; source)
  • Waiver of Administration also applies where the sole heir or beneficiary is appointed administrator, or all heirs/beneficiaries serve or assent. (What is Waiver of Administration? | NH Judicial Branch; source)

Where does probate happen in New Hampshire?

New Hampshire probate runs through the Probate Division of the Circuit Court, with probate judges sitting in courthouses in each of the state's ten counties. The Probate Division handles wills, trusts and estates, guardianships, adoptions, name changes, and equity matters such as partition and quiet title.

Estates that began electronically are e-filed at every probate location. The court's single toll-free number for the Circuit Court is 1-855-212-1234. Contested matters can be sent to a free probate mediation program, which matters if heirs disagree about whether to keep or sell the house.

The court supervises the estate, while the deed for any sale is recorded with the register of deeds in the county where the land lies.

What are the main steps of a New Hampshire estate?

The court appoints an executor or administrator, who then inventories assets, pays debts, and distributes what is left. The Judicial Branch's estates self-help page points to its "Administering an Estate" booklet as the guide for fiduciaries.

  • A will, if there is one, and an application for appointment are filed with the Probate Division.
  • The fiduciary files an Inventory within 90 days after appointment, under RSA 554:1.
  • Debts, funeral costs and administration expenses are paid in the order RSA 554:19 sets.
  • The estate is closed by an accounting, a summary administration, or, for qualifying estates, a waiver of administration.

The Judicial Branch also notes a publication fee for estates that require one. It was raised to $55 on December 28, 2021, so check the current fee when you file.

What goes on the inventory when the estate owns a house?

Real estate is listed with its address, county, book and page from the Registry of Deeds, and an estimated value. The court's inventory overview says town tax records may be used as the estimate, an appraiser is not required unless the court orders one, and the amounts need not be exact.

Values are as of the date of death, and jointly held property is not listed. If the estimate turns out to be significantly off, the fiduciary can file an amended inventory or correct it in the accounting. The total also matters because it can affect the bond the court has already set.

If you plan to sell, a realistic value on the inventory helps later. A sale price far from the inventory figure invites questions from heirs and the court.

Can an executor sell the house, and does the court have to approve?

An administrator needs a court license to sell real estate when the personal estate is not enough to pay debts and legacies. RSA 554:17 requires the administrator to apply for the license, and neglecting to do so is treated as maladministration and a breach of the bond.

The court's Motion and License to Sell Real Estate to Pay Debts form shows how it works in practice. The fiduciary lists the property by county, book and page, totals the debts and assets, and states the shortfall.

  • The motion asks to sell at public auction or private sale.
  • A surviving spouse can assent to the sale, including the homestead right. If there is no spouse but minor children, a guardian of the minors consents.
  • The order's license is valid for two years from the date of the order.
  • A return of sale goes to the court within one year of the sale, and net proceeds are reported within 30 days of receipt.

RSA 554:33 adds that no such license issues later than two years after the executor or administrator was appointed. If the estate has plenty of cash and the will gives the executor power to sell, the path can differ, so ask the court or an attorney which route fits.

What is waiver of administration, and how does it help a seller?

Waiver of administration is a simplified process under RSA 553:32 that skips the inventory, the fiduciary bond and the accounting. The Judicial Branch explains it on its page, "What is Waiver of Administration?", and Justia's copy of RSA 553:32 lists who qualifies.

  • A will names one beneficiary who is appointed administrator, or all beneficiaries serve together, or a trust is the sole beneficiary.
  • There is no will and one heir, including a surviving spouse, is appointed, or all heirs serve together or consent to an appropriate person.
  • The court finds waiver appropriate.

The administrator closes the estate by filing an affidavit of administration between 6 months and 1 year after appointment. The statute sets no value cap and does not exclude real estate, but the affidavit has to list all real estate the decedent owned at death, with its location, book and page. It also has to state that, to the administrator's knowledge, there are no outstanding debts.

Waiver does not erase the duty to pay expenses and debts from estate assets. Any interested person may petition for full administration before the affidavit is filed.

How long do creditors have to make claims against a New Hampshire estate?

The statute keeps creditors on a short clock once an administrator is appointed. Under RSA 556:1, no action can be sustained against an administrator within six months after the original grant of administration, and not unless the demand has been shown to the administrator. Under RSA 556:5, suit must begin within one year after the original grant, with exceptions where the administrator has retained estate in hand.

ItemRuleSource
InventoryWithin 90 days after appointmentRSA 554:1, court inventory overview
Waiver affidavit6 months to 1 year after appointmentRSA 553:32
License to sell real estateNot issued later than 2 years after appointmentRSA 554:33
License validity2 years from the orderCourt form NHJB-2136-Pe
Suit against administratorWithin 1 year of original grantRSA 556:5
Creditor action on real estate if no administrationBarred after 2 years from deathRSA 556:29

RSA 556:29 says that if no administration was granted within two years of the date of death, no creditor can afterward maintain an action to reach the real estate. The details are fact-specific, so ask an attorney before relying on it.

Is there a New Hampshire inheritance or estate tax on the house?

No. The Department of Revenue Administration says the Legacy and Succession Tax was repealed for deaths on or after January 1, 2003, and that the New Hampshire estate tax return is not required for deaths on or after January 1, 2005. Details are on the DRA inheritance and estate tax page.

The real estate transfer tax also has an exemption for inherited property. The DRA's transfer tax FAQ lists transfers by devise, by intestate succession and descent, and by the death of a joint tenant as exceptions. A later sale to a buyer is a different matter. That sale is taxable at $.75 per $100 of the price, paid by both buyer and seller, and the DRA says each side buys stamps from the register of deeds in the county where the property is located.

How does a fiduciary deed work when the estate sells?

The executor or administrator signs a fiduciary deed, which RSA 477:30 sets out in a statutory form. By signing, the fiduciary covenants that he or she was duly authorized to make the sale and followed the statute in doing so. The deed must be acknowledged, and it has to show the grantee's mailing address, under RSA 477:3.

A cash buyer can often work around a slow estate because the sale is as-is and does not depend on a lender's appraisal. Even so, the court steps above still apply. We buy houses in New Hampshire from estates and can coordinate with your attorney on timing, and we do not give legal advice.

More questions about New Hampshire Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property

Which court handles probate in New Hampshire?

The Probate Division of the Circuit Court, with probate judges serving courthouses in each of the ten counties. It handles wills, trusts, estates, guardianships and related equity matters.

How soon after appointment must the inventory be filed?

Within 90 days after appointment, under RSA 554:1. The inventory lists real estate with its county, book and page and an estimated fair market value, and town tax records may be used as the estimate.

Does an executor need court permission to sell inherited real estate?

If the personal estate is not enough to pay debts and legacies, an administrator must apply for a license to sell under RSA 554:17. The court's license is valid for two years, and no license issues later than two years after appointment.

Is there a way to skip the inventory and accounting?

Yes, in qualifying cases. Waiver of administration under RSA 553:32 skips the inventory, bond and accounting, and the estate closes with an affidavit filed between 6 months and 1 year after appointment.

Does New Hampshire have an inheritance tax?

No. The Legacy and Succession Tax was repealed for deaths on or after January 1, 2003, and no estate tax return is required for deaths on or after January 1, 2005.

Is the transfer tax owed when heirs receive the house?

No. Transfers by devise, intestate succession or the death of a joint tenant are exceptions to the real estate transfer tax. A later sale to a buyer is taxable at $.75 per $100, paid by each side.

Can heirs mediate a dispute over the house?

Yes. The Probate Division has a mediation program in which probate-trained mediators can be assigned at no charge to the parties in contested matters.

Selling a New Hampshire House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

This guide covers what official sources say about New Hampshire tax on a house sale.

What the official sources say

  • NH does not have an income tax on an individual's reported W-2 wages. (Interest & Dividends Tax | NH DRA; source)
  • The Interest and Dividends Tax was repealed for taxable periods beginning after December 31, 2024. (Interest & Dividends Tax | NH DRA; source)
Selling in New Hampshire?
We buy New Hampshire houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Does New Hampshire tax the gain when you sell a house?

The New Hampshire Department of Revenue Administration (DRA) pages we opened list no state tax on the gain from selling a house. The state does not have an income tax on an individual's reported W-2 wages, and its Interest and Dividends Tax has been repealed.

That leaves two other layers to plan for. The federal government taxes gain on a home sale unless an exclusion covers it, and New Hampshire charges a real estate transfer tax on the sale itself. If you want to be certain about your own return, call the DRA Taxpayer Services Call Center at (603) 230-5920 or ask a tax professional, because this guide is general information.

  • State: no income tax on wages, Interest and Dividends Tax repealed
  • State: real estate transfer tax on the sale, paid by both sides
  • Federal: capital gain tax on any gain above the home sale exclusion
  • Local: property tax prorated or paid at closing

What was the Interest and Dividends Tax, and is it gone?

The Interest and Dividends (I&D) Tax was a tax on interest and dividend income, and it was repealed for taxable periods beginning after December 31, 2024. It was never a tax on the sale price of a home.

People often mix it up with a capital gains tax because it was New Hampshire's only tax that reached investment income. The DRA's own page summarizes the rate history:

Taxable periodI&D Tax rate
Ending before December 31, 20235 percent
Ending on or after December 31, 20234 percent
Ending on or after December 31, 20243 percent
Beginning after December 31, 2024Repealed

The DRA points to Technical Information Release 2025-001 for the repeal and says the law is found in RSA 77 and Rev 900. If you are filing a final I&D return for an earlier period, the state's Granite Tax Connect portal is where those returns are filed.

How does the federal home sale exclusion work for a New Hampshire seller?

If you sell your main home, the IRS lets you exclude up to $250,000 of gain, or up to $500,000 on a joint return. You have to pass both an ownership test and a use test.

You meet the ownership test if you owned the home for at least 24 months out of the five years before the sale. You meet the use test if you lived in it as a residence for at least 24 months of those five years. The two periods do not have to be the same 24 months. On a joint return, either spouse can meet the ownership test, but both must meet the use test.

  • You generally cannot claim it if you excluded gain on another home during the two years before this sale.
  • If you receive Form 1099-S, you must report the sale even if all the gain is excludable.
  • Report on Form 8949 and Schedule D when required.
  • Military, Foreign Service and intelligence-community members on qualified extended duty can elect to suspend the five-year period for up to 10 years.
  • Publication 523 has the full rules, worksheets and exceptions.

An installment sale does not remove the exclusion. The IRS says it remains available even if you spread the gain over later years.

What federal capital gains rates apply above the exclusion?

A gain on a home held more than one year is long-term and is taxed at 0, 15 or 20 percent for most sellers, depending on taxable income. A gain on a home held a year or less is short-term and taxed as ordinary income.

The IRS lists thresholds for taxable years beginning in 2025. We did not open a page with 2026 thresholds, so treat these as the most recent we could confirm.

RateSingleMarried filing jointly
0 percentUp to $48,350Up to $96,700
15 percent$48,350 to $533,400$96,700 to $600,050
20 percentAbove $533,400Above $600,050

The IRS notes a few exceptions. The part of a gain tied to unrecaptured section 1250 gain on real property is taxed at a maximum of 25 percent, which can matter if you rented the house and took depreciation. People with significant investment income may also owe the net investment income tax, and a large gain can require estimated tax payments.

If you sell at a loss on a personal home, the IRS says the loss is not tax deductible.

How is the gain calculated when the house was inherited or improved?

Gain is the amount you realize from the sale minus your adjusted basis. Basis is generally your cost, plus improvements that add value, minus items such as allowable depreciation.

The IRS says that if you received the property by gift or inheritance, your basis is figured under different rules, and it points to Publication 551, Basis of Assets, for them. We did not open that publication, so we do not state a step-up amount here. Get a date-of-death value from an appraisal and keep it with the estate papers, because that record is what a tax preparer will ask for.

  • Improvements: new roof, additions, major systems. Keep receipts.
  • Selling costs: ask your preparer which closing costs reduce the amount realized.
  • Holding period: the IRS notes that property acquired from a decedent has special holding-period rules, covered in Publication 544.

What New Hampshire tax do sellers actually pay at closing?

The real estate transfer tax is $0.75 per $100 of the price or consideration, and both the buyer and the seller pay it. For a sale of $4,000 or less, each side pays a $20 minimum.

The DRA says the tax is governed by RSA 78-B and Rev 800. Buyer and seller buy stamps from the register of deeds in the property's county, and the register attaches them to the deed when it is recorded.

Within 30 days after the deed is recorded, both parties file their Declaration of Consideration (CD-57-P for the purchaser and CD-57-S for the seller) and the Inventory of Property Transfer (PA-34) with the state. Filing and payment can be done through Granite Tax Connect.

  • Taxable: sales, foreclosure deeds, deeds in lieu, sheriff's sale deeds, leases of 99 years or more
  • Exempt: gifts, transfers between spouses under a final divorce decree, corrective deeds, transfers to the state, a county or a municipality, and transfers by devise, intestate succession or a joint tenant's death

How does property tax fit into a New Hampshire sale?

New Hampshire's property tax year runs April 1 to March 31 under RSA 76:2, and taxes are assessed on the April inventory. Whoever owns the house on April 1 appears on the assessment, and the closing agent settles the split between buyer and seller.

Late taxes carry 8 percent interest under RSA 76:13. If a municipal tax lien is recorded, RSA 80:69 sets 14 percent interest per year on the recorded lien and lets anyone with a legal interest in the land redeem it before the collector gives a deed. The sale proceeds usually clear it through the title company.

For city specifics, our Manchester and Nashua guides cover those offices and dates.

What should you do before selling a New Hampshire house with a large gain?

Work out your basis and your exclusion before you sign, because those two numbers decide whether any federal tax is due. A seller who lived in the house for two of the last five years and has a gain under $250,000 may owe nothing federally, though the IRS still requires reporting in some cases.

  1. Gather the purchase closing statement and improvement receipts.
  2. Count your months of ownership and residence in the last five years.
  3. Check whether a 1099-S will be issued.
  4. Ask a preparer about estimated tax if a taxable gain is likely.
  5. Budget for the 0.75 percent transfer tax on your side.

A cash sale does not change these rules. It changes the timeline, so you can plan when proceeds arrive against any estimated tax payment your preparer expects.

More questions about New Hampshire Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House

Does New Hampshire have a capital gains tax?

The DRA pages we reviewed show no state tax on gain from a home sale. New Hampshire has no income tax on W-2 wages, and the Interest and Dividends Tax was repealed for periods beginning after December 31, 2024. Federal tax can still apply.

How much gain can I exclude on a house sale?

Up to $250,000, or $500,000 on a joint return, if you owned and lived in the home for at least 24 months of the last five years. The IRS also bars the exclusion if you used it on another home in the prior two years.

Who pays the New Hampshire real estate transfer tax?

Both buyer and seller pay it, at $0.75 per $100 of the price. Transfers by will, intestate succession and a joint tenant's death are exempt.

Do I report a home sale if I owe no tax?

Yes, if you receive Form 1099-S, the IRS says you must report the sale even when the gain is excludable. You also report it if you cannot exclude all the gain.

Is a loss on a personal home deductible?

No. The IRS states that losses from the sale of personal-use property, such as your home, are not tax deductible.

Deeds are recorded with the county office named in the sources below.

What the official sources say

  • Recording fee is $10 for the first page plus $4 for each additional page; mortgage discharges $15 first page. (RSA 478:17-g, I; source)
  • An additional $25 LCHIP surcharge applies to recording each deed, mortgage, mortgage discharge or plan; the grantee pays it on a deed. (RSA 478:17-g, II(a); source)
  • Transfer tax is paid by stamps bought from the register of deeds in the county where the property lies, then the deed is recorded. (Real Estate Transfer Tax FAQ | NH Department of Revenue Administration; source)
